title: Trigger Finger: Why a Finger Catches or Locks and What Helps
metaDescription: A finger that catches, clicks or locks is often trigger finger. Learn the causes, first steps, when injection or surgery is considered, and warning signs.
intro: A finger or thumb that catches, clicks or locks in a bent position is usually trigger finger. A tendon (the cord that links muscle to bone) thickens and cannot glide smoothly where it passes through a tight tunnel at the base of the finger. It can sometimes get better on its own, and simple steps often help. An examination of the hand is usually enough to confirm it.

sections.heading: What does trigger finger feel like?
sections.body: The main sign is a finger or thumb that catches, pops or gets stuck in a bent position. You may feel a tender lump on the palm side at the base of the finger, and pain when bending or straightening it. Sometimes you need pressure from the other hand to straighten it. The ring finger and thumb are most often affected.

sections.heading: Why is it worse in the morning?
sections.body: Stiffness and locking are usually worse after inactivity, such as when you wake up. They often ease with gentle use through the day. The tendon or a small nodule (lump) on it has thickened, and the tunnel it slides through has narrowed, so there is less room for it to glide. Cooking, using tools and sport can make it worse.

sections.heading: Who gets trigger finger?
sections.body: It is most common in women aged 40 to 60, and in people with diabetes or rheumatoid arthritis (a joint disease). Repeated gripping or pinching at work or in hobbies may play a part. Often there is no clear cause at all, and it starts without any change in activity. It affects about 2 in 100 people.

sections.heading: What is our usual approach to treatment?
sections.body: We start with the gentlest steps and tailor them to you.
bullets: Medicines first: ibuprofen or naproxen can ease pain and swelling. Paracetamol is an option if you cannot take them.
Rest and splint: avoid repeated gripping and pinching for a while. A night splint keeps the finger straight while you sleep.
Stretching: once pain eases, gentle stretching can reduce stiffness and improve movement.
Physiotherapy machines such as ultrasound or short-wave: if used, these are for pain relief only, and the evidence for them is modest.

sections.heading: Is a steroid injection worth considering?
sections.body: If simple steps do not help, a steroid injection at the base of the finger can reduce swelling and pain, and in many cases it resolves the problem. It can be repeated: up to three injections may be given if symptoms do not improve or return after a time. It is less likely to work in people with diabetes, when triggering has been present for a long time, or in the thumb. In people with diabetes on insulin, blood sugar may rise for about 10 to 14 days. We offer it only to selected people, for pain relief.

sections.heading: Will I need surgery?
sections.body: Often not. Surgery is considered when symptoms are severe, other treatments have not helped, or the finger is stuck bent and cannot be straightened. It is a same-day procedure under local anaesthetic (numbing medicine) that opens the tight tunnel to give the tendon more room. Complications are rare but include infection, stiffness and the problem returning. The wound usually heals within a few weeks, and swelling and stiffness can take 4 to 6 months to settle. We explain your options, and the decision is yours.

sections.heading: When should I see a doctor quickly?
sections.body: Get assessed promptly if your finger locks bent and you cannot straighten it even with the other hand. Also come in if symptoms stop you doing usual daily activities, or after an injury to the finger. Redness, heat, swelling or fever around the finger can be a sign of infection and needs prompt attention.

faqs.q: Can trigger finger get better without treatment?
faqs.a: Yes, it can sometimes improve on its own. Avoiding activities that make it worse until it settles can help.
Usually not. The diagnosis is normally made from your symptoms and an examination of the hand.
A night splint keeps the finger straight while you sleep. It is one of the usual first steps, along with rest from repeated gripping.

faqs.q: Can the problem come back after an injection?
faqs.a: It can. Symptoms sometimes return after a period of time, which is why up to three injections may be used if needed.

faqs.q: Does diabetes make trigger finger harder to treat?
faqs.a: Diabetes raises the risk of getting it, and injections are less likely to work. If you have diabetes, tell us so we can plan your care.
Rarely. Some babies are born with a thumb that locks bent, which is a separate type needing its own assessment.
